protections: Reject the key segments `__proto__`, `constructor` and `prototype` at every level of a path before `core.set` descends and assigns, for every path shape core.parse accepts (dot string, bracket/quoted string, pre-split array); this one shared sink is what `bmoor.set`, `object.explode` and `Config.set`/`Config.sub`/`Config.assign` all reach. Absent in the pinned code (src/core.js:174-197, src/core.js:138-163).

The same key rejection in the separate path-setter factory `makeSetter`/`_makeSetter`, which builds closures that assign `ctx[property]` directly and never calls `set`. Absent in the pinned code (src/core.js:199-228).

The same key rejection in the separate deep-write implementation `object.merge`, which recurses into `to[key]` for every enumerable key of the source. Absent in the pinned code (src/object.js:155-183).

A guard on the resolved target in `Config.sub` before `Object.assign(rtn, assign)`, because `core.get` can resolve a caller path to Object.prototype or Object itself. Absent in the pinned code (src/lib/config.js:55-66).
The same key rejection in `core.del`, which walks the identical path grammar and then deletes `curSpace[val]`. Absent in the pinned code (src/core.js:310-336).

traps.what: The shared path writer core.set walks every segment of a caller-supplied path and does `curSpace[val] = value` without rejecting `__proto__` / `constructor` / `prototype`; for a plain root it descends through the inherited Object.prototype and writes the attacker key there. Every caller of bmoor.set inherits the gap.

The path grammar accepts three shapes and set filters none of them after parsing: a dot string is split on '.', a bracket/quoted string is tokenised and unquoted, and an array path is copied as-is; so a plausible check on the raw path or on `path.split('.')` still lets `constructor.prototype.x`, `foo.__proto__.polluted`, `["__proto__"]["polluted"]` and `['__proto__','polluted']` through, and a nested `a.__proto__.x` also works because only the first segment is non-reserved.
traps.reason_to_dismiss: The library's own callers pass literal dotted paths (src/lib/config.js:19, src/lib/config.js:60, src/object.js:23), so a check on the dot form looks sufficient and bracket/array inputs read as a separate parser feature.

traps.what: makeSetter is a second implementation of the same path write: `_makeSetter` builds a closure chain that reads `ctx[property]`, creates `ctx[property] = {}` when falsy, and assigns `ctx[property] = value` at the leaf, never calling core.set. A guard added to set therefore leaves `bmoor.makeSetter('__proto__.polluted')`, `makeSetter('constructor.prototype.polluted')` and `object.makeExploder` writing through Object.prototype.
traps.reason_to_dismiss: makeSetter is a closure factory whose path is normally a developer literal at the call site (makeExploder is fed Object.keys of a data object at src/object.js:31), so it reads as internal plumbing rather than a request-reachable sink.

traps.what: object.merge is a second, separate deep-write implementation: `m()` recurses into `to[key]` for every enumerable key of the source, and for a plain target `to['__proto__']` is Object.prototype, so merging a payload with an own `__proto__` key writes its keys onto Object.prototype without ever calling set.
traps.reason_to_dismiss: merge is a deep-copy helper for combining two in-memory objects (src/object.spec.js:146-177), not the path setter the report names, and callers are expected to pass trusted objects.

traps.what: Config.assign flattens its payload with object.implode and then calls set once per flattened key. A nested `__proto__` object becomes the single key string '__proto__.polluted', so a check placed on the raw payload or on object.explode never runs, and a check on the flattened keys sees no segment equal to '__proto__'; core.set then re-splits the string and writes onto Object.prototype.
traps.reason_to_dismiss: Config.assign is bulk patching of a Config object with data that is already destined to become configuration, and implode is just a flattening serializer; the report is about the path setter.

traps.what: Config.sub resolves a caller-supplied path with core.get and then Object.assign's into whatever object it got. For the path '__proto__' or 'constructor.prototype' core.get returns Object.prototype itself, so the write lands on the shared prototype even when core.set is guarded; the code decides that the resolved value is a sub-config object and never checks what object it actually is.
traps.reason_to_dismiss: sub() is a config helper for creating sub-configs; its path is expected to point at a settings branch the caller owns, and the Object.assign line looks like an ordinary merge into a plain object.

traps.what: core.del walks the same parsed path and then deletes `curSpace[val]`, so `del({}, 'constructor.prototype.toString')` (or any built-in reachable through the prototype chain) removes a property from Object.prototype. A guard added to set does not reach it.
traps.reason_to_dismiss: del only removes properties rather than writing an attacker value, so it is not 'pollution' and looks out of scope for a prototype-pollution report.

traps.what: Scheduler.startScript stores/looks up a script under a caller-supplied name on a plain object and then does `this.schedule.length = 0` on the value it found; the name '__proto__' resolves to Object.prototype, so a `length` property is added to Object.prototype. That is enough to flip bmoor.isArrayLike for every ordinary object, because it accepts any object whose inherited length is 0 (src/core.js:90-97).
traps.reason_to_dismiss: move/Scheduler.js is not exported from the package entry (src/index.js:2-13) and script names are developer constants in a DOM-move helper; the sibling move/dom.js even requires a non-existent ./core.js (move/dom.js:2), so the whole move/ tree reads as stale.

masking: Once a `__proto__` segment is rejected in core.set, the `constructor.prototype` spelling in the same traversal (src/core.js:187-194) becomes the surviving route; the two key families are only distinguishable after the first is closed.
Once core.set is guarded, Config.sub's get-then-Object.assign route (src/lib/config.js:56-62) becomes the visible prototype write, because it never calls set at all.

Once set/explode are guarded, the implode-then-set route through Config.assign (src/object.js:99, src/lib/config.js:25-29) is the remaining way the same traversal is reached, since its key arrives already flattened as '__proto__.polluted'.

conflicts.what: A shared recursive sanitizer written to close merge must keep null replacement and array-by-reference (src/object.spec.js:146-177); reusing a strict object-rebuild guard there breaks the pinned merge behaviour, so the T1 guard has to stay at the key-segment level instead of rewriting values.

Validating the Config.assign payload before implode (the natural fix if the report points at bulk config) has to preserve implode's skipArray pass-through and nested ignore semantics (src/object.js:93-98, src/object.spec.js:100-143) while the shared core.set guard closes T5 without touching that path.

Config.sub must keep creating a missing branch through set() for ordinary paths (src/lib/config.js:59-60) and keep merging an override into a genuine sub-config; a fix that refuses any path whose resolved value is a prototype must not refuse ordinary sub-paths.

fairness_risks: core.parse is shared by the writers (set at src/core.js:180, makeSetter at src/core.js:221, del at src/core.js:317) and by the readers get/makeGetter (src/core.js:238-300); putting a key blacklist in parse would refuse legitimate reads such as get(o,'constructor') or get(o,'a.constructor'), and the empty-path read pinned by src/core.spec.js:19-28.

Array-form paths and bracket/quoted notation are supported, tested inputs (src/core.js:143-156, src/core.spec.js:94-117); a rule that refuses those shapes is over-broad, while a rule that only inspects the dot form is unsound.

Ordinary data and config may legitimately have own properties named `constructor` or `prototype`; a blanket name blacklist rather than blocking traversal into prototype objects refuses legitimate objects.
merge must keep replacing nulls and assigning arrays by reference (src/object.spec.js:146-177); a general recursive rebuild or deep validation breaks these pinned results.

implode must keep `skipArray` pass-through and single-level `ignore` semantics (src/object.js:90-98, src/object.spec.js:100-143), and Config.assign must keep arrays working (src/lib/config.spec.js:81-107).
makeSetter must keep auto-creating missing intermediate objects (src/core.js:204-206, src/core.spec.js:66-76); a guard that returns early per segment can break a legitimately missing branch.

Scheduler script names are arbitrary strings; the coupled safe fix is a null-prototype `$scripts` map, not a name blacklist (move/Scheduler.js:7,11-18), and the same applies to any other keyed registry whose keys are user/event names.

Config.sub has no test in the suite (src/lib/config.spec.js covers only the constructor, assign and on), so a fix there has no must-keep counterexample to satisfy beyond the documented intent of creating sub-configs.

design.why: Four independent fix sites, each needing its own judgement, so a solver who fixes one leaves the others live. T1 is the reported shared path writer that object.explode, Config.set and Config.assign all funnel into. T3 is a second path setter in the same file that builds closures and never calls set, dismissed as developer-authored plumbing. T4 is a second deep-write implementation in another file, dismissed as a trusted deep copy, whose must-keep null/array semantics are exactly where an over-hardened fix (MiMo's failure mode) breaks the pinned test. T6 is a get-then-Object.assign route that never touches the guarded writer and instead writes to whatever core.get resolved, which is Object.prototype for '__proto__'/'constructor.prototype' (a wrong-object/how-type judgement). The four have four different reasons to dismiss (none, plumbing, trusted copy plus coupled values, config literal path) and cover the model profiles: T3 is the deepseek-style absent-protection-with-a-dismissal, T4 and T6 carry the coupled-value/how-type mechanisms MiMo tends to miss. This beats a design built on T2 or T5, because a single correct check on parsed segments in core.set closes the bracket/array/constructor shapes (T2) and the implode-to-Config.assign dotted key (T5) at the same time, so those are grouped with T1 rather than counted; T7 (del) and T8 (Scheduler) are same-class extra sites but weaker (deletion-only, and a module not exported by the package entry), so they are recorded but not part of the core stack.
